newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Lawmakers worried by trade legislation delay.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Lawmakers worried by trade legislation delay.

text.p: Members of the influential Senate Finance Committee said on Tuesday they were worried that a White House decision to delay trade negotiation legislation will doom chances of enactment over the next couple of years.

Lawmakers said they had hoped to be working this spring on so-called fast track trade negotiation authority that would clear the way for talks to bring Chile into the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA). But the White House decided to put off submitting legislation to Congress until September.

"I think that by delaying action until the fall the president runs the risk that we will not be able to complete fast track this year or next year," Committee Chairman William Roth, Republican of Delaware, said at a panel hearing.

Sen. Daniel Patrick Moynihan, Democrat of New York, told U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky at the hearing that the administration needed "to get on the fast track" with the legislation and he was concerned presidential politics were playing a major role in the decision to delay.
"If this is being held up because of the politics of the New Hampshire primary in the year 2000, that is a dishonorable act," Moynihan said.

The chief opponenent of NAFTA and fast track, House Democratic Leader Richard Gephardt of Missouri, is considered the leading rival to Vice President Al Gore for the Democratic party's nomination for president in 2000 and New Hampshire will be the first major battle ground in that contest.

Barshefsky defended the administration's decision to delay legislation until September, saying debates over a balanced budget agreement between the White House and Congress and over China's Most Favored Nation (MFN) trade status will occupy lawmakers and the president until then.

In an indication of the stiff battle coming on trade with China, Senate Foreign Relations Committee chairman Jesse Helms and three other senators on Tuesday cited Beijing's human rights record when they introduced a resolution to block renewal of its MFN trade status.
"When a country like China gets normal trade relations with the United States, it is getting better treatment than it deserves," the North Carolina Republican said in a statement on the Senate floor.

He called the administration's policy toward's China "an abject failure," and added: "Abject means both 'utterly hopeless' and 'shamelessly servile'. Which, it seems to me, fairly sums up the situation."

Barshefsky, speaking before the China MFN resolution was introduced, said the administration wanted to submit the fast track legislation when President Clinton was able to devote a considerable amount of his time promoting it.
"There is no question the White House is committed to fast track," Barshefsky said. "There is no question it wants to achieve fast track in 1997."

Fast track would allow U.S. officials to negotiate trade agreements with other countries without fear they will be changed by Congress. Lawmakers give up their right to amend trade agreements and can vote only for or against them.

U.S. trade negotiators have been without fast track authority since 1994 and the business community, looking to expand trade with Chile and other Latin American countries, has been pushing for legislation.
Barshefsky said some 20 trade agreements around the world have been concluded without the participation of the United States.
"Increasingly the rules are being written without us," she said.
